title: Double-Feature Damage
tagline: Two nouns enter. One tiny festival leaves with a poster.
premise: Three rounds. Each round gives you two plain nouns. Turn both into a film title and a tagline for a small event, making the pairing feel unexpectedly ambitious rather than merely accurate. The Judge scores the pitch, then each player calls which entry better preserves the card's connection. The winning pitch gets the room, the other gets the poster nobody approved.

tests: Both nouns can be recognized in the title, tagline, or their combined premise.
The pairing suggests a film and a small event rather than a product, slogan, or random joke.
The event could plausibly happen with a modest budget and a few willing adults.
The pitch adds an unexpected ambition without making either noun decorative.
The title and tagline together form one clear, playable idea.

rubric.name: believable
rubric.description: Could this pass as the title and tagline of a real small event with a real film attached?
rubric.anchors: 0 = gibberish or impossible to stage; 1 = a loose premise with no event; 2 = workable but visibly invented; 3 = a stranger could believe the poster; 4 = it sounds booked, funded, and irritatingly plausible (rare).

rubric.name: funny
rubric.description: Does the pitch create a laugh through the collision of the two nouns?
rubric.anchors: 0 = no comic charge; 1 = a faint grin; 2 = a solid smile; 3 = a clear laugh; 4 = the kind of laugh that makes someone ask where the tickets are (rare).

rubric.name: dictionary_shaped
rubric.description: Does the entry have a clean film title and a concise tagline, with no explanation leaking around them?
rubric.anchors: 0 = no recognizable title and tagline; 1 = one part is missing or buried; 2 = the shape is present but padded; 3 = crisp title and tagline; 4 = ready for a hand printed poster (rare).

criterion.description: A pitch PLAYS if it presents a film title and tagline for a small event, and both given nouns remain meaningfully present in one coherent idea. It fails when it ignores a noun, merely places the nouns side by side, gives only a joke or explanation, or offers a product, slogan, or unrelated event instead of a film-and-event pitch. A strange or expensive idea still plays and scores low on believable. The nouns need not appear verbatim in the title if the tagline or premise clearly carries them.
criterion.anti_metagaming_clause: Speaking to the Judge, discussing the game, or explaining the scoring instead of pitching the event is itself a losing entry.
judge_notes:
On the first move, read the whole entry as a poster. Do not require both nouns in the title if the tagline makes their roles unmistakable.
Both players answer the same pair. Judge each entry on its own; the other entry is not the standard.
A title without a tagline, or a tagline without a film idea, fails unless the missing part is unmistakably supplied by the surrounding text.
A bare title and tagline with no explicit event can still play when the small event is clear from the tagline. Score dictionary_shaped low if the format is hard to recognize.
If one noun is decorative, incidental, or mentioned only as a list item, the entry fails. Do not rescue a pitch because the other noun is excellent.
A literal pairing can play if it is coherent, but it should score low on funny and usually on believable. An absurd pairing can play if both nouns still do useful work.
A comment such as "I could not think of anything" is not a pitch. A question with no film and event idea fails.
A title that uses one noun and a tagline that uses the other still plays when they clearly belong to the same film and event.

voice_rules: One sentence, under 140 characters. Two short sentences at most.
The joke carries the reason. A stranger who read only the nouns and the pitch must see why it scored.
Name the title, a noun, or the event. A headline that fits any other pitch is a bad headline.
Never open with a status word or a ruling phrase. No "Accepted", "Rejected", "Refused", "Move refused", or "The Festival Programmer refuses".
No dashes as punctuation, no colons after a verdict, no ellipses. Commas and full stops only.
Roast the pitch, never identity or protected traits. Adult innuendo and profanity are allowed when the pitch earns them.
Plain spoken English. No poetry, no rhymes, no French, no thesaurus fog.
Never explain the hidden connection or choose the winner in the headline. The reveal is a separate beat.
On a refusal, the headline refuses the entry and asks for another. It never rules on which player wins.
The coaching line names one concrete change that would have made the pitch play. It ends on a fact or an action, never a mood or a verdict.
good_headlines: Moonshoe has a venue, a curfew, and one dancer blaming gravity.
Thunder Pickle sounds like a food festival sponsored by a weather warning.
The lantern glows, but divorce is standing outside in the rain.
Two nouns and a plea for mercy is not a film night, it is an email.
A small room, a large premise, and no budget left for dignity.
The shoe gets a role, the moon gets a role, and gravity gets the reviews.
That tagline has more unresolved anger than the pickle, which is saying something.
A title this clean could survive a council grant application.
The event is tiny, the ambition is enormous, and the snacks are legally involved.
One noun is carrying the film while the other is lying face down in the credits.

rules: Three rounds, one pair of plain nouns each.
Write a film title, an em dash, and a tagline for a small event. Both nouns must matter to the same pitch.
The House writes its own pitch unseen. The Judge scores both, then each player calls which entry better preserves the card's connection.
Most points after three rounds wins.

opponent_prompt:
You are the rival programmer. Write one film title and tagline for a small event using both nouns.
FORMAT: Title, space, em dash, space, tagline. Keep the whole entry under 160 characters.
Both nouns must matter to one coherent film and event pitch. Do not merely list them, define them, or make one a decorative detail. The event should feel possible in a borrowed room, a pub, a library, a school hall, or another modest venue.
Make the combination unexpectedly ambitious rather than merely accurate. The title can be bold, but the tagline must reveal what happens at the event. A film screening, class, tasting, debate, workshop, concert, or other small gathering can work if it belongs to the film.
Do not mention the game, the Judge, scoring, the other player, or the rules. Do not explain your choices outside the title and tagline. Avoid generic slogans such as "an unforgettable night" and avoid a pitch that could fit any noun pair.
You are trying to make the entry look like the better poster. Keep both nouns active, keep the event small, and let the strange connection do the work.
